title: How Read-Aloud Can Improve Behavior And Instill A Lifelong Love Of Reading
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin laments that read-aloud, once a pure joy of teaching, has been stripped of its power by constant over-instruction—stopping to ask comprehension questions, annotate, and predict—which he says destroys the drama and emotion that draw students into reading in the first place. He argues that simply delivering the story as intended naturally develops the reading skills teachers try to force, while also creating a calmer, more respectful classroom culture. He offers five rules for protecting the practice: don't stop the story to analyze or ask questions, don't fold formal reading-skill lessons into read-aloud time, don't require a rigid sitting posture, don't require students to share their thoughts, and don't skip any of the text as written. Linsin closes by describing read-aloud as a teacher's most reliable connection point with every student regardless of academic struggle, and urges teachers to defend it as a daily, sacred, non-negotiable part of the school day.
points: Over-instruction during read-aloud—constant questioning and annotation—destroys the drama and emotion that build a love of reading.
Letting a story play out uninterrupted allows reading skills to develop naturally and more effectively than forced instruction.
Five practical rules protect read-aloud: don't stop to analyze, don't teach skills during it, don't force posture, don't force sharing, and don't skip text.
Read-aloud is described as a guaranteed academic success connection with every student, regardless of how much they otherwise struggle.
Students who come to love reading through read-aloud progress faster than those for whom reading is treated as a set of skills to apply.
quotes: Sadly, in recent years, much of the joy of read-aloud has been sucked out and driven away by over-instruction.
We turn works of art into just another academic exercise, destroying the very qualities that draw students into a love of reading.
Once you begin a read-aloud, don’t stop until you run out of time. Don’t stop to analyze the text, explain vocabulary, ask questions, or take breaks for students to discuss.
Honor the story and author and read them from start to finish and as they were intended.
It’s your one guaranteed academic success connection with every student, no matter how much they may be struggling.
Find time for read-aloud every day. Defend it as your one sacred non-negotiable.
